title: Who comes to the faith, and why
source_text: Οἴεται δ᾿ ὅτι τοιαῦτα εἰς προτροπὴν τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων φαμὲν ὡς μηδένα ἄνδρα τῷ ὄντι χρηστὸν καὶ δίκαιον προσάγεσθαι δυνάμενοι, καὶ ὅτι διὰ τοῦτο τοῖς ἀνοσιωτάτοις καὶ ἐξωλεστάτοις τὰς πύλας ἀνοίγομεν. ἡμεῖς δὲ, εἴ τις κατανοήσαι ἡμῶν εὐγνωμόνως τὸ ἄθροισμα, πλείονας ἔχομεν παραστῆσαι τοὺς οὐκ ἀπὸ χαλεποῦ πάνυ βίου, ἤπερ τοὺς ἀπὸ ἐξωλεστάτων ἁμαρτημάτων ἐπιστρέψαντας. καὶ γὰρ πεφύκασιν οἱ τὰ κρείττονα ἑαυτοῖς συνεγνωκότες, εὐχόμενοι ἀληθῆ εἶναι τὰ κηρυσσόμενα περὶ τῆς ὑπὸ θεοῦ τοῖς κρείττοσιν ἀμοιβῆς, ἑτοιμότερον συγκατατίθεσθαι τοῖς λεγομένοις παρὰ τοὺς πάνυ μοχθηρῶς βεβιωκότας, ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ τοῦ συνειδότος κωλυομένους παραδέξασθαι ὅτι κολασθήσονται ὑπο τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι δικαστοῦ κολάσει. ἥτις πρέποι ἂν τῷ τὰ τοσαῦτα ἡμαρτηκότι καὶ οὐ παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον προσάγοιτο ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι δικαστοῦ. ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε δὲ κἂν πάνυ ἐξώλεις παραδέξασθαι βούλωνται τὸν λόγον τὸν περὶ κολάσεως, διὰ τὴν ἐπὶ τῇ μετανοίᾳ ἐλπίδα ἐπιμόνως βεβαμμένοι κωλύονται ἀπὸ τῆς πρὸς τὸ ἁμαρτάνειν συνηθείας, ὡσπερεὶ δευσοποιηθέντες ἀπὸ τῆς κακίας καὶ μηκέτι δυνάμενοι ἀπ᾿ αὐτῆς ἀποστῆναι εὐχερῶς ἐπὶ τὸν καθεστηκότα καὶ τὸν κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον βίον. τοῦτο δὲ καὶ ὁ Κέλσος ἐννοήσας οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως λέγει ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς τοιαῦτα· καὶ μὴν παντί που δῆλον ὅτι τοὺς μὲν ἁμαρτάνειν πεφυκότας τε καὶ εἰθισμένους οὐδεὶς ἂν οὐδὲ κολάζων πάντῃ μεταβάλοι. μήτι γε ἐλεῶν· φύσιν γὰρ ἀμεῖψαι τελέως παγχάλεπον· οἱ δ᾿ ἀναμάρτητοι βελτίους κοινωνοὶ βίου.
pass_a_gloss: He supposes (οἴομαι) that we say such things for the exhortation (προτροπή) of those sinning, as being unable to bring over (προσάγομαι) any man really (τῷ ὄντι) good (χρηστός) and just, and that for this reason we open the gates (πύλη) to the most unholy (ἀνοσιώτατος) and most abandoned (ἐξωλέστατος). But we, if one would consider (κατανοέω) fair-mindedly our gathering (ἄθροισμα), can present (παρίστημι) more who turned (ἐπιστρέφω) from a not very harsh (χαλεπός) life than from most abandoned sins (ἁμάρτημα). For those conscious (σύνοιδα / συγγιγνώσκω, pf.) to themselves of better things, praying (εὔχομαι) that the things preached (κηρύσσω) about the reward (ἀμοιβή) from God to the better be true, are by nature readier to assent (συγκατατίθεμαι) to what is said than those who have lived very wickedly (μοχθηρῶς), hindered (κωλύω) by the conscience (τὸ συνειδός) itself from accepting (παραδέχομαι) that they will be punished (κολάζω) by the Judge (δικαστής) over all with a punishment (κόλασις) which would befit one who has sinned so much and would not be applied (προσάγω) contrary to right reason (ὀρθὸς λόγος) by the Judge over all. Sometimes, even if the utterly abandoned wish to accept the teaching (λόγος) about punishment because of the hope (ἐλπίς) upon repentance, persistently dyed (ἐπιμόνως βάπτω, pf. pass.) they are hindered by the habit (συνήθεια) toward sinning, as if indelibly dyed (δευσοποιέω) by vice and no longer able to stand away (ἀφίστημι) from it easily (εὐχερῶς) to the settled (καθίστημι, pf.) life and that according to right reason. Celsus too, having perceived (ἐννοέω) this, I know not how, says in what follows such things: 'And indeed it is plain to everyone that those by nature (πεφυκότας) sinning and accustomed (ἐθίζω, pf.) no one even punishing would wholly change (μεταβάλλω); much less pitying (ἐλεέω); for to exchange (ἀμείβω) nature completely is all-hard (παγχάλεπος); but the sinless are better partners (κοινωνός) of life.'
pass_b_english: He supposes that we say such things to exhort sinners because we are unable to win over any man who is truly good and just, and that for this reason we open our gates to the most unholy and abandoned. But if anyone would consider our assembly fairly, we can point to more who have turned from a life that was not very bad than who have turned from the most abandoned sins.

For those who are conscious of better things in themselves, and who pray that what is preached about God's reward to the better may be true, are naturally readier to assent to what is said than those who have lived very wickedly. These are kept by their very conscience from accepting that they will be punished by the Judge of all with a punishment that would befit one who has sinned so greatly, and that the Judge of all would inflict without going against right reason. Sometimes, too, even if the utterly abandoned wish to accept the teaching about punishment because of the hope set on repentance, they are held back by their habit of sinning. Long steeped in it, and stained fast by vice, as it were, they can no longer easily turn away from it to a settled life, a life according to right reason.

Celsus too grasped this, I do not know how, and in what follows he says: "And yet it is surely plain to everyone that no one could completely change those who are naturally inclined to sin and accustomed to it, not even by punishing them, much less by showing mercy. For to change nature completely is exceedingly hard. But those without sin are better partners in life."

choices.choice: No Scripture quotation or clear allusion. The TEI punctuation breaks the long second sentence with full stops after κολάσει and before μήτι γε; both are read as continuing the preceding sentence (ἥτις ... refers back to κολάσει; μήτι γε ἐλεῶν completes Celsus's clause). οὐ παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον is kept as a negative ('without going against right reason'): the punishment is fitting and not unreasonable, not one the Judge would withhold. κἂν ... βούλωνται is concessive ('even if they wish'). In that clause διὰ τὴν ἐπὶ τῇ μετανοίᾳ ἐλπίδα is taken with βούλωνται; it could instead be taken with what follows, but that gives poor sense. ἐπιμόνως βεβαμμένοι and δευσοποιηθέντες are dyeing images (a stain set fast); kept as such ('steeped', 'stained fast'). The opening sentence reports Celsus's view indirectly and is not put in quotation marks; the final passage is Celsus quoted directly. Celsus's sentence about those 'naturally inclined to sin and accustomed to it' recurs in 3.66-68 and is worded the same way each time.
'to urge sinners on' -> 'to exhort sinners' (εἰς προτροπήν, matching 3.62)

Judge clause rewritten: 'a punishment the Judge of all would not inflict contrary to right reason' read as if he would withhold it; now 'that the Judge of all would inflict without going against right reason' (keeps οὐ παρά, fixes sense)
κἂν ... βούλωνται rendered as concessive 'even if ... wish', not 'wish ... and yet'
Stiff 'They are dyed in it lastingly' recast as 'Long steeped in it, and stained fast by vice, as it were, they can no longer easily turn away'

Celsus's quoted sentence put in natural English order ('no one could completely change those who ...'), 'even by punishing' -> 'not even by punishing'; 'by nature inclined' -> 'naturally inclined' for consistency with 3.66-68
